title: The Scheduling Problem
summary: Interpret a production job-size distribution under both job-count and GPU-time views.

blocks.md:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Interpret a production job-size distribution under both job-count and GPU-time views
- Distinguish productive GPU-equivalents from raw hardware replaced when valuing a utilization improvement
- Classify jobs as rigid or malleable by workload semantics rather than by domain label

blocks.source: Vol II, Fleet Orchestration, § The Scheduling Problem
blocks.md: Consider two research teams sharing a 1,000-GPU cluster: Team A submits a 512-GPU job that will run for a month, while Team B submits hundreds of 8-GPU experiments that each run for an hour. If the scheduler continually admits whichever jobs fit, Team B's small experiments can indefinitely block Team A's large training run. The scheduling problem is to resolve this conflict among throughput, fairness, and cluster utilization.

blocks.title: What the section covers
blocks.md: Pay attention to: Job-count versus GPU-time views of the production job-size mix; Productive GPU-equivalents versus raw GPUs replaced when utilization improves; Rigid versus malleable jobs as a property of workload semantics.

blocks.prompt: Think first: A 10,000-GPU cluster raises utilization from 50 percent to 80 percent with no new hardware, holding useful work per active GPU-hour constant. Why does the gain count as 3,000 productive GPU-equivalents but replace 6,000 raw GPUs, and when does it become a cash saving?
blocks.md: The productive gain is 10,000 times 0.30, or 3,000 fully utilized GPU-equivalents of useful work. Procurement asks how much hardware that gain replaces: new GPUs run under the old policy would also reach only 50 percent utilization, so delivering 3,000 productive equivalents would take 6,000 raw GPUs. The recovered capacity becomes cash only when it avoids a planned purchase or reduces billed resource time; otherwise it is more useful work from the same investment.

questions.q: In the Kalos language-model cluster trace, most jobs requested a single GPU yet consumed a tiny share of GPU time, while jobs of 256 or more GPUs were a few percent of submissions and consumed nearly all GPU time. What does this distribution imply for judging a scheduling policy?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C. Counted by jobs, the cluster is a stream of small experiments whose users feel queue delay; counted by GPU-hours, it is a few large gangs that decide packing, reservation, and preemption. A policy tuned to either view alone harms the other. Job count alone ignores where the capacity goes, GPU-hours alone ignores most users' experience, and the trace shows this mix is the normal production case rather than an artifact.
questions.hint: Think about: interpret a production job-size distribution under both job-count and GPU-time views.
options: Judge the policy by job count alone, because most users submit small jobs.
Judge the policy by GPU-hours alone, because large jobs hold nearly all of the capacity.
Judge the policy under both views, because small jobs set most users' waits while a few large gangs hold most of the capacity.
Treat the distribution as an artifact of one cluster, because production fleets have uniform job sizes.

questions.q: Whether a job must be scheduled as a rigid gang follows from whether it is labeled an ML training job or an HPC job.
questions.explanation: False. Rigidity is a property of the execution graph, not of the workload's field. Rigid synchronous jobs in either domain need a fixed set of co-scheduled ranks, while malleable jobs can progress across a declared range of resource counts. The scheduler must model each job's minimum viable gang and permitted resize points.
questions.hint: Think about: classify jobs as rigid or malleable by workload semantics rather than by domain label.

points: You can now interpret a production job-size distribution under both job-count and GPU-time views.
You can now distinguish productive GPU-equivalents from raw hardware replaced when valuing a utilization improvement.
You can now classify jobs as rigid or malleable by workload semantics rather than by domain label.
